Rocky relationships in Devil’s Glen Provincial Park

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:09
Instaread
Tensions over rock climbing in the Ontario park are running high — and 1,000 pages of emails show how it got so bad

By Leah Borts-Kuperman

Leah Borts-Kuperman (Local Journalism Initiative Reporter) is based in North Bay, Ont., and focuses on issues affecting what's known as the near north.

Oct. 16, 2026
*|MC_PREVIEW_TEXT|*
BECOME A MEMBER | SUBSCRIBE TO THIS NEWSLETTER
This spring, more than 1,000 pages of emails, made public through freedom of information requests, landed on my desk. There was lots to unpack: angry exchanges between rock climbers, neighbours, ecologists and Ontario Parks staff, over how and where rock climbing should be allowed on a fragile stretch of Niagara Escarpment in Devil’s Glen Provincial Park.

I sifted through allegations of violent threats, screaming matches and racial slurs, old-growth cedars sawed off, cars egged and climbing routes sabotaged. As I talked to sources, trying to understand how a dispute over a recreational activity had become so fraught, it was clear: the story wasn’t “climbers versus neighbours.” It was about what happens when the government ignores scientists, leaving everyone else to deal with the fallout.
 
🔗 Tensions climb in Devil’s Glen

In 2023, Ontario Parks installed signs to keep climbers off 23 routes, of more than 140. Government scientists identified these areas as sensitive — home to rare plants, nesting birds and endangered bats. But, after months of outcry from climbers, the signs came down. Then-environment minister David Piccini made that call, the emails show.

An Ontario Parks ecologist named Ron Gould pushed back: “There has been no scientific rationale involved in the removal of the signed protection areas so hopefully we can get those back in place soon,” he wrote in an email. “These ongoing climbing activities within the sensitive areas are likely to cause further user conflicts and impacts to park values.” 

A year later, Gould’s boss sent him an email instructing him to postpone research in the park. This spring, the province listed rock climbing as an officially permitted activity. 

And just last week, I learned Gould, the only protected areas specialist for Devil’s Glen, has since been dismissed from his role. Ontario Parks didn’t respond to my questions about his departure. 

It’s a theme I’ve seen before.

Last month, senior Ontario reporter Fatima Syed and I investigated what’s happening inside the same ministry’s species-at-risk branch, where staff told us scientists have been sidelined and effectively silenced — reducing them to rubber stamps for development. The ministry didn’t answer our questions for either story.

In both cases, the devil’s in the details. I hope you’ll set aside some time to read the full story — and check out stunning photography by Steven Kell and beautiful illustrations by Susan Kao (come for the immersive opening scroll experience, stay for the juicy storytelling!). Even amid the climbing tensions, Devil’s Glen is well worth the visit.

Take care and tread lightly,

Leah Borts-Kuperman
Northern Ontario reporter

Pathfinding


Meanwhile in the Rocky Mountains, senior Prairies reporter Drew Anderson hit the trails for another story about the complicated relationship between humans and parks. 

He travelled to Kootenay National Park to scamper over fallen logs and encroaching brush with members of the Canadian Backcountry Trails Preservation Society, who want the federal government to focus more attention, and money, on hiking routes. 

But budget shortfalls, crowded tourist zones and the need to protect fragile ecosystems all complicate what some say is a straightforward request. Check it out.
